summary: Describes the procedure for defining new DHCP options. It sets out rules so new options are consistent and well documented. It is a Best Current Practice and was replaced by RFC 2939.

eli5.summary: DHCP hands out settings to computers. This describes how to add a new kind of setting to its list in a proper way.

questions: how to define new dhcp options
what is the procedure for new dhcp options
subtitle: The procedure for adding new options to the DHCP protocol.

tldr.problem: DHCP needed clear rules for how to define and allocate new options so the option space remained organized and well-documented.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2489 establishes a procedure: authors write option specifications as Internet-Drafts, submit them for IESG review, and only after publication as an RFC does IANA assign the actual option code.
tldr.outcome: New DHCP options are allocated through IETF consensus, properly reviewed, and well-documented. Option numbers 1-127 are public (require review) and 128-254 are private-use. This RFC was replaced by RFC 2939.

today: RFC 2489 is a Best Current Practice. It has been replaced by RFC 2939.

sections.title: Defining DHCP Options
sections.content:
The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) lets servers give configuration information to hosts. Configuration data is carried in options: tagged data items in the DHCP message. New options must be defined carefully so that the option code space remains organized and implementations can interoperate.

RFC 2489 describes the procedure to define new options. It ensures that allocation is coordinated, new options are reviewed for correctness, and documentation is complete and published.
sections.eli5: DHCP is like a server handing out instruction cards to computers. Each card type gets a number. This explains how to create new card types.

sections.title: The Option Space and Ranges
sections.content:
The DHCP option number space (1-254) is split into two parts. Public options (1-127) are 'Specification Required': new options need review and IETF consensus before assignment. Site-specific options (128-254) are 'Private Use': organizations can define these locally without IETF review.

Before RFC 2489, the public option space was running out of numbers because option codes were assigned before full specification. RFC 2489 delays assignment until publication as an RFC.
sections.eli5: Numbers 1-127 are official and need approval. Numbers 128-254 are for local use. Each option gets a number only when the RFC is published.

sections.title: Steps to Define a New Option
sections.content:
An author devises the new option and documents it as an Internet-Draft, marking the code as 'To Be Determined'. The author submits the draft to the DHC Working Group or directly to the IESG. The option specification is reviewed by the IESG, and if accepted, it is published as an RFC (standards-track or non-standards-track). At publication time, IANA assigns the option code.

The procedure ensures that new options are not used in products or other specifications before the RFC is published. This protects the option space and guarantees that all options are properly documented.
sections.eli5: Write the option specification in a draft. Send it to the IETF. If they approve, it becomes an RFC and IANA gives it a number. Do not use it before then.
